title: Should you size a market from the buyers' side or the sellers' side?
description: Market sizing for case interviews. "How big is the market for X?" Say your approach before any maths. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: Size a market from whichever side you can estimate with more confidence, then use the other side to check your answer. For most consumer products that means starting from the buyers; for markets limited by capacity, or with a few countable sellers, start from the sellers.
body:
The two directions

Every market sizing question can be built from the people who buy or from the businesses that sell. Say which you are using before any maths, so the interviewer can agree or redirect you.

Demand side (start from buyers)

  1. Population or households
  2. × share in the target segment
  3. × share who buy
  4. × units bought a year (or ÷ years between purchases)
  5. × price, if you need value

Supply side (start from sellers)

  1. Number of sellers, sites or workers
  2. × sales or capacity each, per day or year
  3. × price, if you need value

Which side to start from

Start from buyers whenStart from sellers when
The buyers are a population you can picture (households, drivers, dog owners)Sellers are few and countable (airports, cinemas, car factories)
Purchase habits are easy to reason aboutCapacity limits the market (hairdressers, dentists, hotel rooms)
The question is about potential demandThe question is about what is actually sold today

The London hairdressers example uses both: haircuts needed (demand) divided by haircuts one person can do (supply).

A worked example

"How many home coffee machines are sold in the UK each year?" First, decide what counts: new machines sold this year, not machines already in kitchens, and not the capsules that go with them.

Demand side. About 28M UK households. Assume 40% own a coffee machine: 11.2M machines in use. If a machine lasts six years, replacements are 11.2M ÷ 6 = about 1.9M a year. First-time buyers would add to this.

Supply side. Assume 20 large retailers (online and high street) sell 60,000 machines each, which is 1.2M, plus 3,000 smaller shops and online sellers at 200 each, which is 0.6M. Total: 1.8M.

The two land within about 4% of each other, so you can state "roughly 1.8 to 1.9 million a year" with confidence. These are illustrative assumptions for practice, not market statistics. At an average price of $150, that is about $280M a year.

Which assumption matters

The useful question is not which method is "correct", but which assumption your answer depends on. If machines last eight years rather than six, demand falls to 11.2M ÷ 8 = 1.4M, a 25% drop. Tell the interviewer that machine life drives the estimate and how you would test it, for example by asking a retailer how often customers replace.

How it sounds in an interview

"I could size this from buyers or sellers. I'll start with households, because I can reason about ownership and how long a machine lasts. Then I'll cross-check with retailer sales. If the two are far apart, one of my assumptions is wrong, and I'll say which I trust more."

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a side you cannot estimate. If you have no feel for how many shops sell scooters, do not start there.
  • Mixing stock and flow. Machines in kitchens are a stock; machines sold this year are a flow. Divide the stock by its life.
  • Skipping the cross-check. One method can be wrong in a way you cannot see from inside it.

Quick practice

Which side would you start from for each of these: daily passengers at Heathrow, UK spending on dog grooming, and piano tuners in Chicago?

Show the answer

Heathrow: sellers, because flights are countable (runway slots × passengers per flight), and passenger behaviour is hard to picture. Dog grooming: buyers, because you can reason about dogs, the share groomed professionally and visits a year. Piano tuners: both, as with hairdressers: tunings needed (demand) divided by tunings one tuner can do (supply).

Practise it
